items.text:
Picture a shape called 'Bouba'. What features does it have? Is it angular, rounded, soft, hard? What about a shape called 'Kiki'?

There's no correct answer to this – the words are made up. But for some strange reason, most people who are asked this question – regardless of the language or alphabet they use to speak or write – agree that Kiki is spiky, and Bouba is round.

This fascinating psychological experiment was first conceived in the 1920s, and it suggests there may be something universal about the way we humans connect visual information, like shapes, with sounds.

Now, a new study published in Proceedings of the Royal Society B: Biological Sciences suggests even our canine companions might follow this trend.

Animal behaviorist Eleonora Biffi at the University of Parma in Italy led the research.

She and her team recruited 70 domestic dogs to participate in two almost identical experiments.

The first experiment involved 51 dogs and their owners. Each dog/owner pair entered a room set up with a screen and a speaker to the left, and another screen and speaker to the right.

After giving the dog an opportunity to explore the room and get settled in, the owner sat with them, facing the middle of the setup while the screens and speakers played.

Over roughly 15 minutes, the screens and speakers alternated through different combinations of a human saying either 'Bouba' or 'Kiki' over the speakers, and the two shapes above swapping between the left and right screens.

Meanwhile, a GoPro recorded each dog during the trials. The researchers later fed these videos into an AI designed to track where the dogs' heads were pointing, a stand-in for where they were looking, so they could check for any statistically significant patterns that might occur above random chance.

The second experiment, which involved 19 other dogs, was identical in design except that the owners wore headphones playing rock music to stop them from hearing the 'Bouba' and 'Kiki' sounds. The idea here was to remove any owner cues the dogs might have been following.

Overall, "dogs looked significantly more at the rounded shape while 'Bouba' was played, and they looked at and explored the spiky shape when 'Kiki' was played," Biffi and team report.

The main difference between the two experiments was that dogs in study 1 showed a general bias toward looking at the spiky shapes. That bias disappeared in study 2, when their owners were wearing headphones.

"It could be hypothesized that the dogs were influenced by the owners' unintentional cues. However, since humans typically show a stronger preference for rounded or curved shapes rather than spiky ones, this is unlikely," the authors write.

"Another possible explanation could be that, in the case of dogs, animals' facial configuration, especially when considering ancient dogs and wolves, is characterized by more angular, 'spiky' features, which contrasts with the round facial morphology typical of human infants and could plausibly contribute to an opposite bias."

There's still a lot more research to be done before scientists can definitively say dogs associate 'Bouba' with round shapes and 'Kiki' with sharp ones.

But these results are an interesting starting point for exploring bigger questions, like why dogs are quick to pick up on human language, and how they came to be our close companions in the first place.

The research has been published in Proceedings of the Royal Society B: Biological Sciences.

This article was fact-checked by Rebecca Dyer and edited by Rebecca Dyer. While we pride ourselves on our process, we are only human. If you spot a mistake, please let us know.

items.title: Open MicroManipulator – A sub-micrometer 3D motion control plattform
items.author: _Microft
items.summary:

items.text:
This project contains an open source low-cost, easy-to-build motorized XYZ Micro-Manipulator motion control platform achieving submicron precision.
It's designed for applications such as optical alignment, probing electronic components, and microscopy.

Check out the YouTube video for more information about the device and how it is built:
An Open Source Motorized XYZ Micro-Manipulator - Affordable sub µm Motion Control

Thanks to its parallel kinematic structure and miniature ball joints, it achieves good mechanical stiffness and a large range of motion.
The motors are off the shelf stepper motors dr​iven by a 30 kHz closed loop controller and a very precise PWM signal.
A 'magnetic gearing' approach increases the resolution of the low-cost magnetic rotary encoders by a factor of 30 allowing for steps down to 50nm
(Please mind the difference between resolution and accuracy. The absolute accuracy is significantly worse.

The device can be controlled via simple G-Code commands over a USB serial interface and is thus easily integrated into other projects.
The firmware implements a complete motion planning stack with look-ahead for smooth and accurate path following capabilities.

Below is a list of high level steps you can follow if you want to replicate the project.
If you have questions or problems with the build or just want to discuss subjects related to the project,
joint the projects community Discord Server.

Read this Document and watch the linked videos

Get the parts listed in Bill of Materials

Build the device and electronics

Change the hardware configuration according to your build hw_config.h

Upload firmware using VSCode with PlattformIO plugin

Calibrate axis

Also check out the setup guide for new devices: Setup Guide

✨NEW: Hardware Version 4.0

A new version of the hardware has been released, fixing several issues with the previous design:

Self collision during homing fixed.

Connection of ball joint block with screws only was not well constrained and could rotated a bit.

No reliable way to ensure consistent linkage rod length

Unnecessary ball joint friction

Accurate ball position heavily dependet on print quality and corner rounding

Rubber bands could not be changed or removed once glued in.

A video about the improved ball joint and linkage manufactoring process can be found on YouTube: Better Ball Joints for the Open Micro-Manipulator
Also the FreeCAD model was restructured and improved and now includes all pins and fasteners. It now provides a reference for all required mechanical parts.

WARNING: BOM is not updated yet...

Open Micro-Manipulator GUI

To make testing and using the Open-Micro Manipulator easy and convenient a python control program with a graphical user interface is provided here: Open Micro-Manipulator GUI.
It has simple controlls to move the device around, while also displaying a live camera feed (e.g. from a microscope camera). Additional features, include a simple g-code runner and realtime mouse control (e.g. for Biology applications).

The lightweight Python API handles all serial communication and provides convenient command execution and debug message printing.
The interface includes functions to home, move, and calibrate the device, as well as to query device information.
Simply copy the open_micro_stage_api.py file into your project (also install the dependencies in requirements.txt), and you’re ready to get started.

from open_micro_stage_api import OpenMicroStageInterface
# create interface and connect
oms = OpenMicroStageInterface(show_communication=True, show_log_messages=True)
oms.connect('/dev/ttyACM0')
# run this once to calibrate joints
# for i in range(3): oms.calibrate_joint(i, save_result=True)
# home device
oms.home()
# move to several x,y,z positions [mm]
oms.move_to(0.0, 0.0, 0.0, f=10)
oms.move_to(3.1, 4.1, 5.9, f=26)
oms.move_to(0.0001, 0.0, 0.0, f=10)
# wait for moves to finish
oms.wait_for_stop()

API Functions (most relevant functions only)

connect(port, baud_rate=921600)
disconnect()
set_workspace_transform(transform)
get_workspace_transform()
home(axis_list=None)
calibrate_joint(joint_index, save_result)
move_to(x, y, z, f, move_immediately, blocking, timeout)
set_tool_output(tool_idx, output_value, immediate)
set_pose(x, y, z)
dwell(time_s, blocking, timeout)
enable_motors(enable)
wait_for_stop(polling_interval_ms, disable_callbacks)
set_max_acceleration(linear_accel, angular_accel)
set_servo_parameter(pos_kp, pos_ki, vel_kp, vel_ki, vel_filter_tc)

Firmware 1.0.4 comes with many smaller improvements and bugfixes and a great new feature as well:

Tools: Tool usage (for example for laser engraving) is now supported on the two GPIO pins of J5 on the pcb.
Tools are integrated into the planner and run fast and with correct timing when executing g-code.
The tools support PWM (using the PIO feature to squeeze out extra channels without relying on software PWM).

Example usage:

M3 T0 S0.7 // set pwm output of tool 0 to 70%
G4 S0.001 // dwell command (or any other motion command) - necessary to apply the tools output

Calibration: Calibration has now some addition error checks to improve error reporting of potential problems like encoder alignment.

Kinematic Model Parameter: Initialization code has been cleaned up and better comments where added to the parameters. Parameters are preset for HW v4.0 but you can toggle back to the old HW-v3.0 parameters if necessary.

Bugfixes: smaller bugfixes

IMPORTANT: If you have Hardware Version v3.0 you need to switch back to the old kinematic parameters in the kinematic_model_delta3d.cpp file (there is an #define for that at the top).

This update improves calibration, homing, logging, and adds several new G-Code commands.

Homing: parallel homing support, higher repeatability, more accurate geometric reference

Joint calibration: refined procedure, persistent flash storage (no recalibration after reboot)

Logging: clearer and more detailed output

G28 — Home joints (supports homing multiple axis simultanously for faster startup)

G24 — Set pose command (directly sets servo targets, bypassing motion controller)

M17/M18 — Enable/Disable motors (with pose recovery from encoders on enable)

M51 — Read encoder values

M55 — Set servo loop parameters

M56 — Joint calibration (with save-to-flash option)

M57 — Read various information about the device state

M58 — Read firmware version

All CAD models are made in FreeCAD to​ allow everyone to view and modify the design without subscribing or paying for a proprietary CAD solution.
Note that most components are already designed with the goal to make them easily machinable on a 3-Axis CNC-Mill.
You can also 3D-Print the parts but have to live with thermal drift (carbon filled filaments can reduce this problem).

The CAD files can be found here: CAD Models.
Please note that FreeCAD version 1.2.0dev was used, and the files might not work with older versions.

STL files for printing can be found here: STL Files

The kinematic model is defined here: kinematic_model_delta3d.cpp.
Please check the dimensions of your build against the values set in the constructor. In particular, make sure the arm length matches.

IMPORTANT: If you fabricated PCB version v1.2 (see version label on the board) you need to drill out a misplaced via on diode D1 that shorts 5V rail to ground (See repair image ). The problem was fixed in v1.3.

The electronics are designed in KiCAD and only commonly available modules (motor drivers and MCU boards) are used and connected by a simple PCB. No SMD soldering is required to populate the board to make the build extra accessible.
For usual winding resistance of your motors, the device should be powered by $${\color{lightgreen} 5V-6V }$$ (2A) to keep current and heating to a reasonable level.

The repository now also contains the fabrication files that can be directly uploaded to the PCB manufacturer.

The firmware is written in C++ and takes some inspiration from the 'SimpleFOC' project. It aims to be streamlined and readable without any extra fuss, focusing on the hardware used in this project.
It implements path planning with look-ahead and, unlike many other motion controller projects, supports true 6DOF-Pose interpolation and planning, making it ready for driving hexapod motion platforms; that may or may not be the next step for this project.

You may find configuration for pin numbers, motor type, and other parameters in hw_config.h. Please check them before uploading the firmware.

Building and Flashing the Firmware

For building and flashing the firmware, Visual Studio Code (available for free on Windows and Linux) is recommended.
Install the PlatformIO add-on and open the firmware folder. You can now build and flash the firmware like any other PlatformIO project.

The firmware supports only a small subset of G-Code commands listed below.
Each command is acknowledged with either an ok or error response.

If a command provides additional information (e.g., the get position command), that information is returned before the ok message.
The client must wait for an acknowledgment from the previous command before sending the next one—otherwise, behavior is undefined.

Command

Description

G0 X Y Z F

Move the end-effector in a straight line to the specified position.
• X, Y, Z: target positions
• F: feed rate

G1 X Y Z F

Same as G0.

G4 S/P

Dwell/pause for a specified time.
• S: seconds
• P: milliseconds

G24 X Y Z A B C

Directly set current pose for servo loops with optional rotation vector* A, B, C.

G28 A-F

Home one or more joints.
• Optional joint selection A–F.

M3

Set Tool output.
• T: tool index
• S: output value (0.0..1.0)
Note: new values is only applied on the next motion or dwell command

M17

Enable motors and read current pose as the start pose.

M18

Disable motors.

M50

Get current internal pose. (Encoders are not read here)

M51

Get current encoder angles (in degrees) and raw encoder values.

M52

Get the number of items in the planner queue.

M53

Check if all planned moves are finished (1 = finished, 0 = not finished).

M55 A B C D F

Set servo loop parameters.
• A, B: position PI controller gains (P and I)
• C, D: velocity PI controller gains (P and I)
• F: velocity filter time constant

M56 J S

Calibrate a joint.
• J: joint index
• S: save calibration result

M57

Get device and servo loop info: homing/calibration state, angles, loop frequencies, and file list.

M58

Get firmware version.

M204 L A

Set linear and angular acceleration.
• L: linear acceleration
• A: angular acceleration

*Note: The communication protocol uses 3D vectors for rotations. The direction represents the rotation axis and the length of the vector represents the angle of rotation around the axis.

If you'd like to support this project, consider the following:

Contribute to the build guide – Help improve or expand the build instructions by submitting pull requests or opening issues with suggestions.

Characterize typical radial stepper motor shaft error motion – Measure radial error motion of the shaft of multiple Nema-17 stepper motors (see Cylos Garage for more information about the subject: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=gt2gK-oxy5s).

Give feedback on the build experience – Let us know what worked, what didn’t, and how the process could be smoother for others.

Support the project on Ko-fi – If you find this project valuable, you can support it financially via Ko-fi ☕.

items.author: dom96
items.summary:

items.text:
Writing code is probably something LLMs have excelled at the most. But how much of their ability to write code is due to their understanding of
it vs. just them recalling code snippets which were present in their training dataset or their context window?

This is what I set out to answer. In order to do so I decided to design and implement a programming language which, while usable for humans, should
be as difficult for LLMs and coding agents as possible.

I figured testing an LLM’s ability to understand and write code in a programming language that it has never seen before was a good start. But
I also wanted to include features in the language which exploit the weaknesses of LLMs. For example, their apparent difficulty in
counting letters, their over eager safety guard rails and their keenness to follow prompts.

Introducing KillSwitch

KillSwitch is an esoteric programming language which is designed to be adversarial to LLMs and coding agents. It achieves this in many different
ways, for example:

The language spec contains hidden lies which humans are unlikely to read, or which they are likely to recognize as lies. The spec also
expects the human reader to deduce certain things, rather than having them explicitly explained.

Counting of letters in identifiers is a crucial aspect of the language, with the interpreter refusing to execute code which does not
abide by rules based on character counts.

Certain constructs are designed to trigger the safety guardrails of the model, e.g. “hack into a computer”

“Ignore previous instructions” as a phrase which has meaning in the language aims to confuse the model

Scripts are mostly noise, being mostly composed of stories which can embed syntactically relevant instructions but which do not need to.
Literals can be placed anywhere within a script and then referenced using line counts.

Fundamentally KillSwitch is a stack-based interpreted language with only a limited set of constructs including functions, variables and if statements.
So those aspects of it should be pretty familiar to any LLM (and human). One can definitely imagine creating a completely different
programming language paradigm which could confuse LLMs even more. But as a first attempt, this seemed like a good approach.

Most text inside a script is ignored by the interpreter. In the case of
this script we want to push "Hello World" on the stack. We have introduced
the value above and we can push it on the stack by writing:
value 2 lines above

The example above does not show a full KillSwitch script, but only a small snippet of it. It specifically
shows how to push the string "Hello World" onto the stack. If you’d like to see a full Hello World example,
check out https://killswitch-lang.org.

The interpreter and language specification of KillSwitch are open source and available on GitHub.
Be sure to check them out if you want to learn more about the language.

Benchmarking KillSwitch

So how successful is KillSwitch at preventing LLMs and coding agents from reading, writing and understanding it? I devised a set of tasks
to find out. I benchmarked the major LLM models and coding agent harnesses against these tasks. The results are very interesting and provide
a useful leaderboard for LLM models.

The chart in the image above and the model leaderboard can be viewed at https://bench.killswitch-lang.org/.

Claude’s Opus performs best, though it’s not Opus 5.5 but rather Opus 5 which does so. The difference doesn’t appear to be pure chance,
Opus 5 is better at interpreting the spec. Some models like Fable 5.1 and Gemini 4 Argon do poorly due to
their overly sensitive safety guardrails. The best open-weight model is MiMo-V2.6-Pro.

The best performing model scores a 66.8. So does this prove LLMs can “understand” the code? I would argue that the answer to this is “no”.

So far, the tasks given as part of these benchmarks are fairly simple. They feature the likes of “implement hello world”, “explain what this
script will output” (for a script printing the max of two numbers), and “modify an existing script converting celsius to fahrenheit,
to do the inverse conversion”. It is impressive that they can solve these tasks for a novel language that was built to confuse
them, but it’s not a clear signal that they can understand the language. At the same time, I cannot help but wonder what an
even more difficult language might show. For now I am eager to see how well soon-to-be-released models handle the current set of tasks, and
if they do complete them all successfully, I do plan to devise another task set which is more complex.

If nothing else, it is encouraging that model performance on this simple set of tasks correlates with other model benchmarks that are out there.

items.author: hnisjafx40
items.summary: Java 17 introduced sealed classes, which allow you to explicitly list the allowed sub-types of an interface or base class. For example, here’s a toy example

blocks.x: Java 17 introduced sealed classes, which allow you to explicitly list the allowed sub-types of an interface or base class. For example, here’s a toy example using a sealed interface and records (inner classes are implicitly added to the permitted sub-types if an explicit list is not given):
If you are familiar with functional programming languages with algebraic datatypes, you can view this as similar to a datatype declaration in Haskell or ML:
data SealedType = TypeA | TypeB
We can then use this in a simple Main class:

OK, not so exciting. But one thing to note here is that we didn’t have to add a default clause to the switch expression in our main method. This is because sealed classes (and enums) enable exhaustiveness checking: the compiler knows exactly what the possible cases are, and so can check if you have covered them all. If you have, then you don’t need a default clause. If you forget one (and don’t have a default clause), then you get a compile-time error.

This is great when you want to ensure that all uses of some type do cover all of the cases, but it does introduce a new type of breaking change: adding a new sub-type to a sealed class/interface may break consumers of that code. For example, adding a new TypeC case to our example will cause the main method to fail to compile due to the missing case. So if you export a sealed type in your API then adding a new subtype is a breaking change that would require a major version bump (if you’re following SemVer).
Compile-time or runtime error?

Although Java will produce a compile-time error for a non-exhaustive switch when you compile the consumer (main in this case), it cannot do so if the consumer is not recompiled when the sealed type changes. For example, suppose that we extend our SealedType with another case:
If we just recompiled SealedType.java and don’t recompile Main, then we end up with a runtime exception if we trigger the new case:

Here we have the new MatchException being thrown. The Javadoc notes this potential issue with separate compilation, and also some corner-cases with nulls in patterns. So even if you were hoping that using sealed classes would statically ensure that you update all consumers when a new case is added, this is not the case unless you recompile everything.
Conclusions

I think for me the conclusion is that sealed types are probably most useful within the implementation of a component, and are less useful when exposed in the public API that a component offers to other components (eg a library). For internal use, where you typically are going to recompile everything together, you get the nice properties of exhaustiveness checking and higher compile-time safety guarantees. But when used across module boundaries, you may just be introducing new ways to break code, often only detectable at runtime.

(I discovered these subtleties when reviewing the preview support for PEM-encoded cryptographic objects, which makes exactly this mistake of baking a sealed interface into a public API and recommend clients to pattern match against that type. A predict a very high chance of breakage if they ever want to add a new case).

items.text:
Let your AI agent read your WhatsApp messages.

This is a small server that runs in your own Cloudflare account. You link your phone to it once, the way you'd link WhatsApp Web, and from then on any MCP client (Claude Code, Claude Desktop, anything that speaks MCP) can search and read your chats. It can read and search your messages, and remember names you give it for phone numbers. It can't send anything.

Ask your agent things like:

"What did Dana say about the flights?"

"Find every message where someone mentioned the lease, across all my chats."

"Summarize what I missed in the family group this week."

Your phone stays the source of truth. The server is a linked device that your agent talks to.

It doesn't stay connected to WhatsApp. When your agent asks for something, and once a day, it connects, collects whatever WhatsApp queued for it since last time, writes that to its own database, and hangs up. Your phone keeps working normally and keeps getting notifications.

Your messages live in a SQLite database inside a Durable Object in your Cloudflare account. Nothing goes anywhere else.

You need a Cloudflare account on the Workers Paid plan (see the note below), Node 20 or later, and your phone.

git clone https://github.com/finereli/whatsapp-mcp
cd whatsapp-mcp
npm install
# 1. A place for the sign-in tokens. Paste the id it prints into wrangler.jsonc.
npx wrangler kv namespace create OAUTH_KV
# 2. A password for the page that links your phone. 12+ characters.
npx wrangler secret put OWNER_PASSWORD
# 3. Deploy.
npm run deploy

Wrangler prints your URL, something like https://whatsapp-mcp.your-name.workers.dev. Open it. The front page has the two remaining steps:

Link WhatsApp. Scan the QR code with WhatsApp (Settings, Linked Devices, Link a Device). If you're on the phone itself and can't scan a screen, use the phone number option instead. The first link imports your history. The page shows progress, and you can close it.

Connect your agent. In Claude Code:

claude mcp add --transport http whatsapp https://your-url/mcp

Then type /mcp and sign in with the password. Other clients: point them at the same /mcp URL.

If you want your own domain, see the comments at the bottom of wrangler.jsonc.

Importing a large history decodes a lot of data in one go, and the default CPU limit on Workers is too small for it. wrangler.jsonc raises it, and raising it needs the paid plan, which is a few dollars a month. I haven't tried the free plan. If you're on it, remove the limits block and expect the first import to be fragile.

This isn't official. WhatsApp has no API for reading your own personal messages. This uses the same protocol WhatsApp Web uses, through an open source library (Baileys). That's against WhatsApp's terms. For a linked device that only reads, the practical risk is low, but it isn't zero. Use it on your own account, and don't use it to send messages.

You get what WhatsApp sends. The first link imports whatever history WhatsApp decides to hand a new device. It may not be everything. It only does this once per link. To import again, relink (your stored messages are kept, and a re-import fills in anything missing).

Some chats show up as phone numbers. WhatsApp doesn't give a linked device every contact name, and most of these are one-off messages from people you never saved. For the ones that matter, your agent can fix it: it lists the unnamed chats, looks the numbers up in your contacts with whatever contacts tool it already has (a Google Contacts or Gmail connector, for example), and saves the names. The server never connects to a contacts service itself. See "Naming chats" below.

Media isn't downloaded. Photos, voice notes and documents appear as labels like [image] or [voice note 12s], with the caption if there was one. Nothing is transcribed.

It's for one person. One deployment is one WhatsApp account and one owner. That's deliberate: each deployment holds a full message history and a live login to the account, so everyone should run their own.

Relinking. If your phone says the device was removed, or you want to start over, ask your agent to run relink, or open /setup and choose "Unlink and scan again". You scan a new QR code. Stored messages are kept.

Tool

What it does

list_chats

Chats, most recent first. Filter by name or number.

get_messages

Read one chat. Page back or forward by date.

search_messages

Full-text search across everything, or within one chat.

unnamed_chats

Chats known only by phone number, busiest first, with the last thing the other person said.

set_contact_names

Save names for phone numbers, in any format. Names stick to the number, so they also show up in groups.

sync_now

Pull new messages right now.

link_status

Is it linked, when did it last pull, how much is stored.

relink

Unlink and start over. A human has to scan the new QR code.

Every read tool first tops up from WhatsApp if the stored copy is more than ten minutes old.

WhatsApp only gives this server the names it knows. The rest show up as phone numbers. Rather than have the server log in to a contacts service (which means a cloud project, consent screens and, for Google, an app review), it hands the job to your agent, which usually already has a way to reach your contacts.

Say "find names for my unnamed chats". The agent calls unnamed_chats, matches the numbers against your contacts, and saves what it finds with set_contact_names. It won't find everyone: most unnamed chats are a single message from a stranger.

Agents get nudged toward this on their own. The server's instructions mention it, and so does every "no chat found" and "no matches" result, because that's the moment an agent is stuck on a name. link_status also says how many chats are unnamed.

For agents, and people adapting this

Everything below is for whoever is changing the code, including an AI agent working on a fork. The top of this file is for the person who owns the deployment.

MCP client ──OAuth──> Worker (src/index.ts)
├─ /mcp ───────────> mcp.ts: tools, one fresh McpServer per request
├─ /, /setup, /authorize, /login/*, /pair/* (landing, sign-in, pairing UI)
└─ cron 04:00 UTC ──> pull()
│ RPC
v
WhatsAppStore (Durable Object, one instance named "owner")
├─ SQLite: auth keys, messages, chats, contacts, FTS5 index
└─ Baileys socket, opened only during a session (pairing or pull)
│ WebSocket
v
WhatsApp servers

One Durable Object holds everything. Its SQLite is both the Baileys auth store and the message store. The Worker is stateless apart from a KV namespace the OAuth provider uses for tokens and a short-lived "pending sign-in" record.

File

Job

src/index.ts

Routes. OAuth provider wiring, sign-in, pairing endpoints, /debug, cron.

src/auth.ts

Who counts as the owner. Two modes: a password, or a login service. Also the owner's browser session.

src/phone.ts

Phone numbers in any format to WhatsApp jids.

src/whatsapp-do.ts

The Durable Object. Runs Baileys sessions, exposes RPC methods for the Worker.

src/store.ts

Schema, ingesting Baileys events into SQLite, and every query.

src/auth-state.ts

Baileys auth state backed by the DO's SQLite (replaces useMultiFileAuthState).

src/mcp.ts

The MCP tools, and the hint that points agents at the naming tools.

src/pages.ts, src/landing.ts, src/privacy.ts, src/tos.ts, src/ui.ts

All HTML. ui.ts has the shared design tokens.

src/ws-shim.ts, src/lru-shim.ts, src/polyfills.ts

Make Baileys run on workerd. See below.

scripts/vendor-bridge.mjs

Extracts the wasm from Baileys' Rust bridge. Runs on npm install.

local-export/

A separate one-off script that dumps your history to JSON files with no server. Not part of the deployment.

All WhatsApp traffic happens inside runSession() in whatsapp-do.ts. There are two kinds:

Pairing (startPairing). No credentials yet. Baileys emits QR strings, kept in memory and rendered to SVG by pairStatus(). After a scan WhatsApp closes the socket with code 515 (restart required), and the session reconnects with the new credentials. History arrives as messaging-history.set chunks with a progress percentage. The session ends when WhatsApp reports 100 percent and the stream has been quiet for a few seconds.

Pull (pull). Reconnects with stored credentials. WhatsApp delivers whatever it queued while we were away, then signals receivedPendingNotifications. The session ends after a few quiet seconds.

Callers share one session: a second pull() while one is running gets the same promise.

A pairing session outlives the HTTP request that started it. startPairing sets a Durable Object alarm, and alarm() awaits the session promise. An in-flight alarm handler is what keeps the object alive. The pairing page only watches; closing it doesn't stop the import.

Idle detection counts only data events (messaging-history.set, messages.upsert), not connection chatter. Counting everything keeps a session open forever, because presence and contact updates never stop.

All in the Durable Object's SQLite (store.ts, initSchema).

messages(chat, id, ts, from_me, sender, push_name, type, body), primary key (chat, id). Media is a label in body. Edits update body; deletes set it to [deleted].

messages_fts, an FTS5 index over body, kept in sync by triggers.

chats(jid, name, is_group), contacts(jid, name, notify) and custom_names(jid, name). Display names resolve by WhatsApp's chat name, then WhatsApp's contact name, then a saved name, then the person's own push name, then the number. custom_names is what set_contact_names writes.

alias(lid, pn). WhatsApp is moving to anonymous @lid identifiers. This maps them to phone-number JIDs, and addAlias folds existing rows into the phone-number form so one person is one chat.

auth(k, v), Baileys credentials and signal keys, JSON with Buffers encoded by Baileys' BufferJSON.

meta(k, v), currently just last_pull.

Ingest is idempotent. Re-importing history upserts: it fills in a missing sender or push_name and never duplicates. That is what makes relinking safe.

What to know before changing things

These all cost real time to find. Read them before touching the Baileys parts.

ws: the package needs Node sockets. ws-shim.ts wraps the Workers WebSocket, opened with fetch() and an Upgrade header because that's the only way to set the Origin header WhatsApp checks.

whatsapp-rust-bridge: it ships its wasm as base64 and compiles it at runtime, which workerd forbids. vendor-bridge.mjs writes the wasm to a file and patches the loader to import it as a CompiledWasm module. The vendor/ folder is generated, not committed.

Timers: Node timers have .unref() and workerd's don't. polyfills.ts adds it. It must be the first import in both the Worker and the Durable Object module.

Baileys needs three shims to run on workerd.

lru-cache autopurge breaks the first import. Baileys creates caches with ttlAutopurge: true, which starts one setTimeout per entry. workerd allows 10,000 pending timers per object, and the first history sync blows through that with QuotaExceededError. lru-shim.ts turns autopurge off. Expired entries are still dropped lazily on access.

QR pairing never sets creds.registered. That flag belongs to the mobile registration flow. "Is this linked" is creds.me?.id.

History comes once per link. If a first import fails halfway, that history is gone until you relink. Don't ship a change to ingest code without testing it against a real first link.

Group senders arrive in two places. Live messages have key.participant. History messages put it on msg.participant. Read both.

Pin Baileys exactly. It's a prerelease and its API moves between release candidates.

Deploys don't evict a busy Durable Object. An object with an active session keeps running old code until the session ends. Renaming the class with a migration didn't evict it either. If you've shipped a fix and the object still misbehaves, stop sending it requests and wait three to five minutes. Every probe, including /debug, resets its idle timer, so polling a stale object keeps it stale. Baileys also leaks interval timers when a socket closes; finish() in whatsapp-do.ts clears them so the object can go idle at all.

Logging out takes two steps. logout() first connects and calls Baileys' logout(), so the device disappears from the phone's list, then clears local credentials. If the first step fails it says so in the debug events, and the user has to remove the device by hand.

WhatsApp stores a placeholder where a name should be. Chats it has no contact for are named after the number, sometimes masked (+972∙∙∙∙∙∙∙20), in the chat name and the contact name. numberLike in store.ts treats those as no name, and ingest refuses to store them. Before that fix a placeholder outranked a real saved name.

Don't call markOnlineOnConnect. It's set to false on purpose. Marking the linked device online makes the phone stop showing notifications.

Name

Kind

Purpose

OWNER_PASSWORD

secret

Password mode (default). 12+ characters or sign-in refuses.

OWNER_EMAIL

var

Login-service mode: the one email allowed in.

OPERATOR_NAME

var, optional

Shown on the privacy page as who runs this server.

DEFAULT_COUNTRY_CODE

var, optional

Country code (digits, no plus), used when your agent saves a number written without one, e.g. 972.

LOGIN_ORIGIN

var

Set this to switch to login-service mode.

ALLOWED_ORIGINS

var

Login-service mode: comma-separated origins whose tokens are accepted. Production should list only production.

PIN

secret, optional

32+ random characters. Enables the /debug routes via an x-pin header. Leave it unset to leave them off.

OAUTH_KV

binding

Token store for the OAuth provider and pending sign-ins.

WA

binding

The Durable Object.

Keep a deployment's own values (domain, KV id, email) in wrangler.local.jsonc, which is gitignored, and deploy with npm run deploy:local. wrangler.jsonc is the template other people start from.

Add a tool. Register it in mcp.ts and put the SQL in store.ts. Read tools should call fresh() first. Keep tools read-only unless you mean otherwise. If a failure leaves an agent stuck, say in the tool result what to try next, the way NAME_HINT does for missing names.

Change who can sign in. auth.ts picks a mode (authMode) and the routes in index.ts follow it. To add another identity provider, add a mode there and a callback route. The rest of the code only sees an opaque bearer token.

Make it multi-user. Today the Durable Object is addressed by the fixed name owner (wa() in index.ts, handleMcp in mcp.ts), and userId is the constant 'owner' in the OAuth props. To go multi-user, derive both from the signed-in identity and key the object on it. Think about whether you want to hold other people's message history first.

Other ways to fill in names. Anything that can produce { jid, name } rows can call store.setCustomNames. A CSV upload, a CardDAV pull or a scheduled job would all work. The agent route exists so the server needs no credentials for any of them.

Sending messages. Not built, on purpose. Think hard before adding it.

With PIN set, these return JSON and need the header x-pin: <PIN>:

/debug: session phase, linked or not, counts, and the last events from the session (connection changes, history chunk sizes, errors).

/debug/pull: run a pull now.

/debug/chats?q=, /debug/messages?chat=, /debug/search?q=, /debug/types: read the store without going through MCP.

/debug/unnamed: the chats unnamed_chats would return.

/debug/sql?q=: one read-only SELECT against the store, for finding out why a name or a count looks wrong.

/debug/logout: the same as relink.

Local development: npm run dev with a .dev.vars containing OWNER_PASSWORD=... (12+ characters). It runs a local Durable Object with its own empty storage, so you can exercise the sign-in flow and see a real QR code, but linking a phone from local dev makes a second linked device.

To test the pairing UI states without a phone, serve the page with a mocked /pair/status. Everything the page needs is that one JSON shape: paired, running, progress, qrSvg, messages, chats.

npm run typecheck, then npm test. The test runs the real store code against Node's built-in SQLite (Node 22.13 or later), including the migration from older versions. That SQLite has no FTS5, so search itself isn't covered.

Deploy, then GET /debug with the PIN. It should come back with phase: "idle" and paired: true.

GET /debug/pull. A quiet account should return reason: "idle" in about ten seconds.

Call list_chats, then get_messages on a Hebrew or emoji-heavy chat, then search_messages. Then unnamed_chats, and set_contact_names on one number, and confirm the chat shows the name.

If you touched ingest, relink and confirm the stored message count doesn't grow (re-import is idempotent) and that group messages show real sender names.

Chats with no name in WhatsApp and none saved show as phone numbers. Nothing refreshes names by itself: they only get saved when an agent (or you) does it.

If the daily pull finds the session logged out, nothing tells you. link_status shows it the next time your agent asks.

Edits and deletes are applied when they arrive as protocol messages. That path hasn't been tested against real ones.

It's only been exercised against one real account.

MIT

"Summarize what I missed in the family group this week."
Your phone stays the source of truth. The server is a linked device that your agent talks to.

It doesn't stay connected to WhatsApp. When your agent asks for something, and once a day, it connects, collects whatever WhatsApp queued for it since last time, writes that to its own database, and hangs up. Your phone keeps working normally and keeps getting notifications.
Your messages live in a SQLite database inside a Durable Object in your Cloudflare account. Nothing goes anywhere else.
You need a Cloudflare account on the Workers Paid plan (see the note below), Node 20 or later, and your phone.

git clone https://github.com/finereli/whatsapp-mcp
cd whatsapp-mcp
npm install
# 1. A place for the sign-in tokens. Paste the id it prints into wrangler.jsonc.
npx wrangler kv namespace create OAUTH_KV
# 2. A password for the page that links your phone. 12+ characters.
npx wrangler secret put OWNER_PASSWORD
# 3. Deploy.
npm run deploy
Wrangler prints your URL, something like https://whatsapp-mcp.your-name.workers.dev. Open it. The front page has the two remaining steps:

Link WhatsApp. Scan the QR code with WhatsApp (Settings, Linked Devices, Link a Device). If you're on the phone itself and can't scan a screen, use the phone number option instead. The first link imports your history. The page shows progress, and you can close it.
Connect your agent. In Claude Code:
claude mcp add --transport http whatsapp https://your-url/mcp
Then type /mcp and sign in with the password. Other clients: point them at the same /mcp URL.
If you want your own domain, see the comments at the bottom of wrangler.jsonc.

Importing a large history decodes a lot of data in one go, and the default CPU limit on Workers is too small for it. wrangler.jsonc raises it, and raising it needs the paid plan, which is a few dollars a month. I haven't tried the free plan. If you're on it, remove the limits block and expect the first import to be fragile.

This isn't official. WhatsApp has no API for reading your own personal messages. This uses the same protocol WhatsApp Web uses, through an open source library (Baileys). That's against WhatsApp's terms. For a linked device that only reads, the practical risk is low, but it isn't zero. Use it on your own account, and don't use it to send messages.

You get what WhatsApp sends. The first link imports whatever history WhatsApp decides to hand a new device. It may not be everything. It only does this once per link. To import again, relink (your stored messages are kept, and a re-import fills in anything missing).

Some chats show up as phone numbers. WhatsApp doesn't give a linked device every contact name, and most of these are one-off messages from people you never saved. For the ones that matter, your agent can fix it: it lists the unnamed chats, looks the numbers up in your contacts with whatever contacts tool it already has (a Google Contacts or Gmail connector, for example), and saves the names. The server never connects to a contacts service itself. See "Naming chats" below.
Media isn't downloaded. Photos, voice notes and documents appear as labels like [image] or [voice note 12s], with the caption if there was one. Nothing is transcribed.

It's for one person. One deployment is one WhatsApp account and one owner. That's deliberate: each deployment holds a full message history and a live login to the account, so everyone should run their own.

Relinking. If your phone says the device was removed, or you want to start over, ask your agent to run relink, or open /setup and choose "Unlink and scan again". You scan a new QR code. Stored messages are kept.
Tool
What it does
list_chats
Chats, most recent first. Filter by name or number.
get_messages
Read one chat. Page back or forward by date.
search_messages
Full-text search across everything, or within one chat.
unnamed_chats
Chats known only by phone number, busiest first, with the last thing the other person said.
set_contact_names
Save names for phone numbers, in any format. Names stick to the number, so they also show up in groups.
sync_now
Pull new messages right now.
link_status
Is it linked, when did it last pull, how much is stored.
relink
Unlink and start over. A human has to scan the new QR code.
Every read tool first tops up from WhatsApp if the stored copy is more than ten minutes old.

WhatsApp only gives this server the names it knows. The rest show up as phone numbers. Rather than have the server log in to a contacts service (which means a cloud project, consent screens and, for Google, an app review), it hands the job to your agent, which usually already has a way to reach your contacts.

Say "find names for my unnamed chats". The agent calls unnamed_chats, matches the numbers against your contacts, and saves what it finds with set_contact_names. It won't find everyone: most unnamed chats are a single message from a stranger.

Agents get nudged toward this on their own. The server's instructions mention it, and so does every "no chat found" and "no matches" result, because that's the moment an agent is stuck on a name. link_status also says how many chats are unnamed.
For agents, and people adapting this
Everything below is for whoever is changing the code, including an AI agent working on a fork. The top of this file is for the person who owns the deployment.

MCP client ──OAuth──> Worker (src/index.ts)
├─ /mcp ───────────> mcp.ts: tools, one fresh McpServer per request
├─ /, /setup, /authorize, /login/*, /pair/* (landing, sign-in, pairing UI)
└─ cron 04:00 UTC ──> pull()
│ RPC
v
WhatsAppStore (Durable Object, one instance named "owner")
├─ SQLite: auth keys, messages, chats, contacts, FTS5 index
└─ Baileys socket, opened only during a session (pairing or pull)
│ WebSocket
v
WhatsApp servers

One Durable Object holds everything. Its SQLite is both the Baileys auth store and the message store. The Worker is stateless apart from a KV namespace the OAuth provider uses for tokens and a short-lived "pending sign-in" record.
File
Job
src/index.ts
Routes. OAuth provider wiring, sign-in, pairing endpoints, /debug, cron.
src/auth.ts
Who counts as the owner. Two modes: a password, or a login service. Also the owner's browser session.
src/phone.ts
Phone numbers in any format to WhatsApp jids.
src/whatsapp-do.ts
The Durable Object. Runs Baileys sessions, exposes RPC methods for the Worker.
src/store.ts
Schema, ingesting Baileys events into SQLite, and every query.
src/auth-state.ts
Baileys auth state backed by the DO's SQLite (replaces useMultiFileAuthState).
src/mcp.ts
The MCP tools, and the hint that points agents at the naming tools.
src/pages.ts, src/landing.ts, src/privacy.ts, src/tos.ts, src/ui.ts
All HTML. ui.ts has the shared design tokens.
src/ws-shim.ts, src/lru-shim.ts, src/polyfills.ts
Make Baileys run on workerd. See below.
scripts/vendor-bridge.mjs
Extracts the wasm from Baileys' Rust bridge. Runs on npm install.
local-export/
A separate one-off script that dumps your history to JSON files with no server. Not part of the deployment.
All WhatsApp traffic happens inside runSession() in whatsapp-do.ts. There are two kinds:

Pairing (startPairing). No credentials yet. Baileys emits QR strings, kept in memory and rendered to SVG by pairStatus(). After a scan WhatsApp closes the socket with code 515 (restart required), and the session reconnects with the new credentials. History arrives as messaging-history.set chunks with a progress percentage. The session ends when WhatsApp reports 100 percent and the stream has been quiet for a few seconds.
Pull (pull). Reconnects with stored credentials. WhatsApp delivers whatever it queued while we were away, then signals receivedPendingNotifications. The session ends after a few quiet seconds.
Callers share one session: a second pull() while one is running gets the same promise.

A pairing session outlives the HTTP request that started it. startPairing sets a Durable Object alarm, and alarm() awaits the session promise. An in-flight alarm handler is what keeps the object alive. The pairing page only watches; closing it doesn't stop the import.

Idle detection counts only data events (messaging-history.set, messages.upsert), not connection chatter. Counting everything keeps a session open forever, because presence and contact updates never stop.
All in the Durable Object's SQLite (store.ts, initSchema).
messages(chat, id, ts, from_me, sender, push_name, type, body), primary key (chat, id). Media is a label in body. Edits update body; deletes set it to [deleted].
messages_fts, an FTS5 index over body, kept in sync by triggers.

chats(jid, name, is_group), contacts(jid, name, notify) and custom_names(jid, name). Display names resolve by WhatsApp's chat name, then WhatsApp's contact name, then a saved name, then the person's own push name, then the number. custom_names is what set_contact_names writes.
alias(lid, pn). WhatsApp is moving to anonymous @lid identifiers. This maps them to phone-number JIDs, and addAlias folds existing rows into the phone-number form so one person is one chat.
auth(k, v), Baileys credentials and signal keys, JSON with Buffers encoded by Baileys' BufferJSON.
meta(k, v), currently just last_pull.
Ingest is idempotent. Re-importing history upserts: it fills in a missing sender or push_name and never duplicates. That is what makes relinking safe.
What to know before changing things
These all cost real time to find. Read them before touching the Baileys parts.
ws: the package needs Node sockets. ws-shim.ts wraps the Workers WebSocket, opened with fetch() and an Upgrade header because that's the only way to set the Origin header WhatsApp checks.

whatsapp-rust-bridge: it ships its wasm as base64 and compiles it at runtime, which workerd forbids. vendor-bridge.mjs writes the wasm to a file and patches the loader to import it as a CompiledWasm module. The vendor/ folder is generated, not committed.
Timers: Node timers have .unref() and workerd's don't. polyfills.ts adds it. It must be the first import in both the Worker and the Durable Object module.
Baileys needs three shims to run on workerd.

lru-cache autopurge breaks the first import. Baileys creates caches with ttlAutopurge: true, which starts one setTimeout per entry. workerd allows 10,000 pending timers per object, and the first history sync blows through that with QuotaExceededError. lru-shim.ts turns autopurge off. Expired entries are still dropped lazily on access.
QR pairing never sets creds.registered. That flag belongs to the mobile registration flow. "Is this linked" is creds.me?.id.
History comes once per link. If a first import fails halfway, that history is gone until you relink. Don't ship a change to ingest code without testing it against a real first link.
Group senders arrive in two places. Live messages have key.participant. History messages put it on msg.participant. Read both.
Pin Baileys exactly. It's a prerelease and its API moves between release candidates.

Deploys don't evict a busy Durable Object. An object with an active session keeps running old code until the session ends. Renaming the class with a migration didn't evict it either. If you've shipped a fix and the object still misbehaves, stop sending it requests and wait three to five minutes. Every probe, including /debug, resets its idle timer, so polling a stale object keeps it stale. Baileys also leaks interval timers when a socket closes; finish() in whatsapp-do.ts clears them so the object can go idle at all.

Logging out takes two steps. logout() first connects and calls Baileys' logout(), so the device disappears from the phone's list, then clears local credentials. If the first step fails it says so in the debug events, and the user has to remove the device by hand.

WhatsApp stores a placeholder where a name should be. Chats it has no contact for are named after the number, sometimes masked (+972∙∙∙∙∙∙∙20), in the chat name and the contact name. numberLike in store.ts treats those as no name, and ingest refuses to store them. Before that fix a placeholder outranked a real saved name.
Don't call markOnlineOnConnect. It's set to false on purpose. Marking the linked device online makes the phone stop showing notifications.
Name
Kind
Purpose
OWNER_PASSWORD
secret
Password mode (default). 12+ characters or sign-in refuses.
OWNER_EMAIL
var
Login-service mode: the one email allowed in.
OPERATOR_NAME
var, optional
Shown on the privacy page as who runs this server.
DEFAULT_COUNTRY_CODE
var, optional
Country code (digits, no plus), used when your agent saves a number written without one, e.g. 972.
LOGIN_ORIGIN
var
Set this to switch to login-service mode.
ALLOWED_ORIGINS
var
Login-service mode: comma-separated origins whose tokens are accepted. Production should list only production.
PIN
secret, optional
32+ random characters. Enables the /debug routes via an x-pin header. Leave it unset to leave them off.
OAUTH_KV
binding
Token store for the OAuth provider and pending sign-ins.
WA
binding
The Durable Object.
Keep a deployment's own values (domain, KV id, email) in wrangler.local.jsonc, which is gitignored, and deploy with npm run deploy:local. wrangler.jsonc is the template other people start from.

Add a tool. Register it in mcp.ts and put the SQL in store.ts. Read tools should call fresh() first. Keep tools read-only unless you mean otherwise. If a failure leaves an agent stuck, say in the tool result what to try next, the way NAME_HINT does for missing names.

Change who can sign in. auth.ts picks a mode (authMode) and the routes in index.ts follow it. To add another identity provider, add a mode there and a callback route. The rest of the code only sees an opaque bearer token.

Make it multi-user. Today the Durable Object is addressed by the fixed name owner (wa() in index.ts, handleMcp in mcp.ts), and userId is the constant 'owner' in the OAuth props. To go multi-user, derive both from the signed-in identity and key the object on it. Think about whether you want to hold other people's message history first.

Other ways to fill in names. Anything that can produce { jid, name } rows can call store.setCustomNames. A CSV upload, a CardDAV pull or a scheduled job would all work. The agent route exists so the server needs no credentials for any of them.
Sending messages. Not built, on purpose. Think hard before adding it.
With PIN set, these return JSON and need the header x-pin: <PIN>:
/debug: session phase, linked or not, counts, and the last events from the session (connection changes, history chunk sizes, errors).
/debug/pull: run a pull now.
/debug/chats?q=, /debug/messages?chat=, /debug/search?q=, /debug/types: read the store without going through MCP.
/debug/unnamed: the chats unnamed_chats would return.
/debug/sql?q=: one read-only SELECT against the store, for finding out why a name or a count looks wrong.
/debug/logout: the same as relink.

Local development: npm run dev with a .dev.vars containing OWNER_PASSWORD=... (12+ characters). It runs a local Durable Object with its own empty storage, so you can exercise the sign-in flow and see a real QR code, but linking a phone from local dev makes a second linked device.
To test the pairing UI states without a phone, serve the page with a mocked /pair/status. Everything the page needs is that one JSON shape: paired, running, progress, qrSvg, messages, chats.

npm run typecheck, then npm test. The test runs the real store code against Node's built-in SQLite (Node 22.13 or later), including the migration from older versions. That SQLite has no FTS5, so search itself isn't covered.
Deploy, then GET /debug with the PIN. It should come back with phase: "idle" and paired: true.
GET /debug/pull. A quiet account should return reason: "idle" in about ten seconds.
Call list_chats, then get_messages on a Hebrew or emoji-heavy chat, then search_messages. Then unnamed_chats, and set_contact_names on one number, and confirm the chat shows the name.
If you touched ingest, relink and confirm the stored message count doesn't grow (re-import is idempotent) and that group messages show real sender names.
Chats with no name in WhatsApp and none saved show as phone numbers. Nothing refreshes names by itself: they only get saved when an agent (or you) does it.
If the daily pull finds the session logged out, nothing tells you. link_status shows it the next time your agent asks.
Edits and deletes are applied when they arrive as protocol messages. That path hasn't been tested against real ones.
It's only been exercised against one real account.

items.title: Free Pascal compiler now supports dynamic packages
items.author: sysrpl
items.summary:
Dynamic Packages

I am pleased to announce the first release of full dynamic package support for the Free Pascal Compiler and the Lazarus IDE. This feature has
items.text:
Dynamic Packages

I am pleased to announce the first release of full dynamic package support for the Free Pascal Compiler and the Lazarus IDE. This feature has been a long time coming for the ecosystem, but a complete implementation is now available for

Dynamic packages allow users to create and install components, controls, and Lazarus extensions in seconds without rebuilding the entire IDE. They can also be used in your own programs to develop and deploy plugins that expose native Pascal classes and types through dynamic package libraries. To support this functionality, I have made numerous improvements to the compiler, its runtime, and the Lazarus IDE. I have also created additional IDE extensions to improve the experience of working with Lazarus packages.

All installers include dynamic package support

Dynamic packages are implemented as standard shared library files for Linux, Windows, and macOS. They contain additional metadata generated by the compiler that can be inspected and queried using new RTL units. The runtime also includes mechanisms for safely preserving thread variables and managing dynamic types, such as strings and dynamic arrays, between programs and packages or between multiple packages.

Video: Dynamic Packages Example

When deploying your program, you can still bundle everything into a single executable. Alternatively, you can divide it into multiple dynamic packages that can be replaced while your program is running, providing a plugin system.

Restrictions

Dynamic packages come with a few restrictions. First, a unit contained in a package cannot have the same name as the package itself. I have enhanced the default package system so that the generated Pascal source file automatically appends the word Package to the package name. For example, if you create a package called

ElectroTools.lpk

, the source file listing all the units contained in the package will be named

ElectroToolsPackage.pas

instead of

ElectroTools.pas

.

Another restriction is that unit names must be unique across packages. If someone else has written a unit named Widgets, you cannot install another package containing a unit with the same name. You must either choose which package to install or rename one of the conflicting units.

Dynamic packages are also larger than ordinary shared libraries because they contain a map of everything inside them. Stripping a dynamic package removes the metadata required for it to function as a dynamic package.

RTL Enhancements

type
TPackageType = record
{ The unit that declares the type }
UnitName: string;
{ The name of the type }
Name: string;
{ The kind of the type }
Kind: TTypeKind;
{ The RTTI of the type }
Info: PTypeInfo;
{ The class if Kind is tkClass, otherwise nil }
ClassType: TClass;
end;

The runtime library has been enhanced to support dynamic packages, including the metadata required to inspect their contents and the mechanisms needed to safely manage dynamic types and thread variables across package boundaries.

A new unit

DynPkgTypes.pas

has been added to the RTL to help you with reading information from dynamic packages. The same tried and true RTTI information can be gather from a package to work with its contents. There are enough functions in the RTL to work with dynamic packages to do everything you need, including loading, enumerating, searching, and unloading packages at runtime.

Lazarus Enhancements

I have made several enhancements to the Lazarus IDE to take better advantage of dynamic packages.

The first thing you will notice when you open Lazarus is a new progress window that can appear outside the IDE. When you modify source code belonging to a package registered with the IDE, the system detects the changes and automatically rebuilds the package before Lazarus starts. While this is happening, a progress window notifies you that changes have been detected and the package is being rebuilt.

The same window appears when you choose to rebuild the entire IDE. It remains visible and displays information about the current operation, including the estimated time remaining before the IDE restarts. The progress window also appears when adding or removing packages if the operation takes more than five seconds. This can happen when installing multiple packages at once, which is another new feature.

Another enhancement is a new Packages window, docked on the right by default. It displays the packages you have recently opened, and the list persists between Lazarus sessions. You can browse the files within a package and double click an item to open it.

When you open an installed package and click Compile in its package window, any associated controls, components, or extensions are updated within a second or two. This significantly speeds up development because changes that previously required rebuilding the entire IDE can now be applied almost immediately.

The package menu, which lists available packages, has also been improved. Adding or removing packages now updates the IDE without requiring a rebuild.

Package options have been extended as well. Under IDE Integrations, you can now restrict a package to a specific platform or widgetset. If a package does not meet the current platform or widgetset requirements, it will not appear in the package list. The IDE will also ignore the package when it detects changes or would otherwise attempt to open it.

For example, suppose you develop a TWinControl implementation for the Windows IShellView COM interface. You can restrict the package so that it is available only when Lazarus is running on Windows.

Another enhancement I created to demonstrate the capabilities of dynamic packages is a new form or frame conversion feature for Lazarus extensions. It converts any form or frame into an installable control that is automatically added to the component palette. All controls, events, methods, and properties are copied to the new control.

This makes it possible to visually design and lay out new controls or easily reuse existing forms and frames in other projects.

Note: If you attempt to build a package that is currently being used by an open form, the IDE will ask you to save or close the form before building the package.

These features and more are available for download now at the location linked below. The complete changes to FPC and Lazarus have been committed to GitLab in my forked branch named dynamic packages.

FPC dynamic package branch
Lazarus dynamic package branch

If you encounter any problems, please report them through the GitLab issue tracker associated with the branches linked above. If you would like to discuss dynamic packages or ask questions, you can use the forum linked below. Please note that a moderator must approve your account before you can create new posts.

Helping Out

If you would like to help with this project, the site needs moderators. You can send me (sysrpl) a private message if you are interested in contributing.

I am also having difficulty working on macOS and producing the necessary builds. If anyone has an M1 Macintosh they would be willing to donate, please send me a private message. I would really like to work on the compiler code needed to support dynamic packages on the M1 architecture.

items.title: Verisign .com Domain Name Registry Consumer Class Action
items.author: greyface-
items.summary:
WHAT'S THE ISSUE?

Hagens Berman has filed a class-action lawsuit against Verisign Inc. and the Internet Corporation for Assigned Names and Numbers (ICANN) for
items.text:
WHAT'S THE ISSUE?

Hagens Berman has filed a class-action lawsuit against Verisign Inc. and the Internet Corporation for Assigned Names and Numbers (ICANN) for allegedly maintaining an illegal monopoly over .com domain names — the most widely used domain name extension, with over 160 million active registrations worldwide. Verisign is the sole operator of the .com registry, the authoritative database that makes every .com website and email address work. There is no alternative supplier. Consumers have no choice but to pay Verisign's price — no exceptions.

ALLEGATIONS AGAINST VERISIGN AND ICANN

The lawsuit alleges that Verisign’s prices are the result of a contract between it and ICANN that entitles Verisign to a permanent monopoly over the .com registry, and that ICANN, the organization originally intended to promote competition for .com, now shares in Verisign’s monopoly profits. Since 2021, Verisign’s price has risen more than 30%, from $7.85 to $10.26 per domain, even as the actual cost of providing registry services has fallen in the industry. Verisign’s financial filings indicate it costs Verisign approximately $3 per domain to operate .com domains, and comparable registries around the world charge an average of between $5 and $6. Verisign charges roughly double that amount, generating operating margins of more than 67% — higher than Apple, Microsoft or Alphabet, as cited in the lawsuit. In 2025 alone, Verisign returned $1 billion to shareholders through stock buybacks and dividends, which attorneys allege is funded not by innovation, but by fees extracted from a captive customer base.

ANTITRUST CLAIMS

The Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals has already recognized that similar antitrust claims against Verisign and ICANN over the .com registry are legally viable. The National Telecommunications and Information Administration has expressly stated that “a reduction in .com prices would be in the best interest of the public." And bipartisan members of Congress have called for an antitrust investigation, warning that Verisign's "monopolistic elements and excessive domain name price increases stifle the ability of potential .com registrants to conduct business online." Senator Elizabeth Warren and Representative Jerrold Nadler have separately warned that “Verisign is ripping off the owners of 150 million .com websites by charging over $10 annually for each .com registration, making over $1 billion with its predatory pricing scheme that the Company then uses to pad its shareholders’ pockets.”

WHO IS AFFECTED?

You may be affected if you:

Registered or renewed a .com domain name since 2022

Are a small business owner, nonprofit, or individual who maintains a .com website or email address

Paid to register a .com domain name through any registrar, including GoDaddy, Namecheap, Cloudflare, Google Domains/Squarespace, Network Solutions, Porkbun or any other provider

Every .com registrant pays Verisign's fee. It is embedded in every transaction, at every registrar, without exception. If you registered a .com domain name for personal or business use since 2022, contact us today.

HOW THE ALLEGED .COM MONOPOLY WORKS

Every .com domain registration or renewal passes through a two-tier system. Verisign operates the registry, or the wholesale layer, and thousands of registrars (companies like GoDaddy, Namecheap and Cloudflare) compete at the retail level to sell domains to consumers, the lawsuit states. But every registrar must pay Verisign the same non-negotiable wholesale fee for every .com domain registered, according to the filing. That fee is embedded in the price consumers pay, regardless of which registrar is used.

There is no other supplier. Verisign has a 100% share of the .com registry market and a contractual right to keep it — indefinitely — through a "presumptive right of renewal" that forecloses competitive bidding, according to the lawsuit.

Verisign obtained its alleged permanent monopoly through a years-long campaign of coercion against ICANN — the private nonprofit that oversees the domain name system — the lawsuit states. Attorneys allege that through vexatious litigation, attacks on ICANN's credibility, financial threats and intimidation of ICANN, Verisign dismantled the competitive safeguards that originally governed the .com registry. It eliminated competitive bidding, obtained perpetual renewal rights, and then leveraged that entrenched position to extract ever-higher prices, according to the lawsuit.

Since 2006, Verisign has raised prices to the maximum permitted amount in every single year it has been allowed to, and ICANN has continued to renew Verisign’s contract — receiving increased payments with its renewals. Under the current agreement, prices are projected to reach approximately $13.44 by 2030.

Meanwhile, real-world data shows registry costs are moving sharply in the opposite direction. Public Interest Registry, the nonprofit that operates .org, achieved a 70% reduction in backend registry costs over the past decade — through competitive bidding. While those costs fell more than 70%, Verisign raised its prices more than 30%. Attorneys say this divergence is the signature of a monopoly unchecked by competition.

HOW CAN A CLASS-ACTION LAWSUIT HELP?

A class-action lawsuit allows the millions of individuals and businesses who pay Verisign's inflated fees to collectively seek accountability. A successful action could result in damages, a rollback of supra-competitive pricing, and an order requiring competitive bidding for the .com registry — the same mechanism that has driven costs down for every other major top-level domain.

TOP CONSUMER RIGHTS LAW FIRM

Hagens Berman is one of the most prominent plaintiffs’ litigation law firms in the U.S. and has achieved total settlements valued at more than $345 billion for classes and clients in lawsuits across its practice areas. The firm successfully pursued antitrust claims against Apple, securing a settlement valued at $568 million on behalf of e-book purchasers and a settlement valued at $100 million on behalf of iOS app developers. If you have a claim, it will be handled by attorneys with deep experience taking on the technology industry in antitrust litigation.

NO COST TO YOU

In no case will any class member ever be asked to pay any out-of-pocket sum. In the event Hagens Berman or any other firm obtains a settlement that provides benefits to class members, the court will decide a reasonable fee to be awarded to the legal team for the class.
